title: Black Holes of All Sizes Follow the Same Rule for Launching Jets
summary:
An international team of astronomers co-led by an IAS scholar has identified what appears to be a universal rule governing one of the most dramatic behaviors of black holes: the production of powerful jets. The researchers found that black holes can launch jets at the same critical stage of their feeding cycle, regardless of their size. That includes "stellar-mass" black holes about ten times the mass of our sun as well as supermassive black holes that are millions of times heavier.

The work was carried out by Andrew Mummery, Martin A. and Helen Chooljian Member (2025-30) in the School of Natural Sciences at the Institute for Advanced Study, and Adelle Goodwin, a Forrest Research Foundation Fellow at Curtin University's International Centre of Radio Astronomy Research in Western Australia.

Published in Nature Astronomy under the title "A universal critical accretion rate for black hole jet formation," the study brings together years of observations across multiple wavelengths. The researchers combined data from telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa, and space. Their focus was on tidal disruption events, which occur when a star passes so close to a supermassive black hole that intense gravitational forces rip it apart. These events gave the team a rare opportunity to watch how a black hole behaves after suddenly receiving a large supply of stellar material.

"We really wanted to figure out this massive puzzle," said Mummery. "Why do some supermassive black holes blast out radio jets right after shredding a star, while others just sit there looking completely dormant, only to suddenly fire up their jets months or even years later?"

Black holes are often compared with cosmic vacuum cleaners, but their feeding behavior is much messier. "When a black hole tears apart a star, it does not swallow everything neatly," Goodwin stated. Some of the stellar material falls toward the black hole, while much of it can be violently expelled into space through powerful outflows. These enormous cosmic "burps" can carry material across vast distances and can significantly affect the evolution of the galaxies that contain them.

Astronomers have long suspected that black holes obey the same basic physical rules even when their masses differ enormously. Confirming that idea has been difficult because changes around supermassive black holes can normally unfold over thousands or even millions of years. Tidal disruption events offer a way around that problem. When a star is destroyed, the resulting feeding episode around a supermassive black hole can evolve over just a few years. That gives scientists a much faster view of processes that would otherwise be extremely difficult to track in real time.

The key insight behind the new study emerged in an unexpected setting. During an astrophysics conference in Madrid, Mummery and Goodwin were talking in a bar when they realized that the same rule known to govern jet production in smaller black holes might also apply to supermassive ones.

To test the idea, the researchers examined twenty tidal disruption events using observations in optical light, ultraviolet light, X-rays, and radio waves. They eventually narrowed the sample to ten high-quality events for which they could reliably determine both the black hole's feeding rate and the timing of its radio outflows. The analysis revealed two separate periods when jets can form. The first occurs early, while the black hole is consuming material at an extremely high rate. The second appears much later, hundreds to thousands of days after the star was initially torn apart. At that later stage, the black hole's feeding rate falls to about two percent of its Eddington limit, the point at which the outward pressure of radiation balances the inward pull of gravity. That two percent threshold is especially important because it is already known to trigger jet formation in much smaller black holes within our galaxy. Finding the same threshold in supermassive black holes suggests that this part of black hole physics works in essentially the same way across an enormous range of masses.
why_it_matters: If the same rule really governs objects ranging from ten-solar-mass black holes to billion-solar-mass giants, then black hole behavior becomes far more predictable — which matters because jets appear to shape galaxy evolution. It also gives students a concrete example of a scaling law: a single relationship that survives across twelve orders of magnitude in mass, which is the sort of thinking that underlies most modern physics.

background_read: Black hole jets are streams of charged particles flung outward at close to the speed of light; the jet produced by the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy M87 is a famous, widely imaged example of the phenomenon. Because these jets can carry energy far beyond their host galaxy, they are thought to influence how galaxies grow and change over cosmic time.

Andrew Mummery works at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey — an independent research institute where Albert Einstein spent the last decades of his life — and Adelle Goodwin is a Forrest Research Foundation Fellow at Curtin University (a university in Perth, Western Australia) and its International Centre of Radio Astronomy Research. Their paper appeared in Nature Astronomy, a peer-reviewed journal that publishes astronomy research.

The two percent figure comes from the Eddington limit, named after Arthur Eddington, a British astrophysicist who studied how radiation pushes outward on matter inside stars. Astronomers use the limit as a standard measuring stick because it lets them compare black holes of wildly different masses on the same scale.

Tidal disruption events are rare and hard to catch — they are usually found by wide-field sky surveys that scan large parts of the sky repeatedly. That rarity is exactly why they are useful: instead of watching a supermassive black hole change over millions of years, astronomers can watch a whole feeding episode unfold in just a few years.

One long-standing puzzle in astrophysics is whether physical laws stay the same across enormous ranges of scale. Finding the same threshold in stellar-mass and supermassive black holes supports the idea of 'self-similar' behavior, in which the same rules apply whether the object weighs ten suns or a billion.

perspectives.description: The study ties together observations gathered by telescopes on several continents and in space, and it links two objects that are otherwise impossible to compare directly: a small black hole in our own galaxy and a giant one in a distant galaxy. If the rule holds, astronomers gain a single predictive framework for when jets switch on, no matter the mass.

The conclusion rests on only ten well-measured tidal disruption events, and the researchers themselves had to discard half of the original twenty for lack of reliable data. Tidal disruption events are chaotic, vary widely, and may not represent how black holes normally feed, so a two percent threshold could be a coincidence of a small sample rather than a universal constant.

Physics has repeatedly found that nature reuses the same relationships at different scales, from pendulums to stars. This result fits that tradition: the two percent figure had already been identified in smaller black holes, and the new work simply asks whether the pattern survives when masses grow millions of times larger. The real test is whether future observations keep landing on the same number.

Wider sky surveys should catch many more tidal disruption events, and upgraded radio and X-ray facilities can track their outflows in far greater detail. If dozens more events cluster around the same threshold, the 'universal rule' label becomes hard to argue with; if they scatter widely, the idea will need revision. Either outcome sharpens how models treat jets and their effect on galaxies.
